function.name: cmd_controller_execute
function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

unit.description: Specifies the unit of measure for the command if applicable. This is not utilized by os.system() directly but can be used for logging or analysis purposes.

message.content:
I don’t have a way to directly probe your connection from here, so I can’t tell you the exact speed right now.  
Here’s what you can do to find out:

| Method | How to use it | Notes |
|--------|---------------|-------|
| **Web speed‑test sites** (e.g., [speedtest.net](https://www.speedtest.net/), [fast.com](https://fast.com/)) | Open the site in a browser and click “Go” or “Start.” | Gives you download/upload speeds and ping. |
| **Command‑line speedtest** (if you have `speedtest-cli` installed) | ```bash\nspeedtest-cli\n``` | Works on Windows, macOS, Linux. If you’re on Windows, you can run it via PowerShell or CMD. |
| **Router’s admin page** | Log into your router’s web interface (usually `192.168.1.1` or `192.168.0.1`) and look for a “Status” or “Diagnostics” section. | Some routers display current throughput. |
| **Mobile apps** | Install the Speedtest app from Google Play or the App Store. | Handy if you’re on a phone or tablet. |

If you’d like, I can help you run a command‑line test on your machine. Just let me know which OS you’re using and whether you have `speedtest-cli` installed.
